title: The background job that was starving the API
question: Tell me about the hardest issue you have debugged

situation: A service responsible for orchestrating and storing Lambda function packages was handed over to our team from the US. Shortly afterwards, we extended it to support high-volume ZIP functions alongside the existing image-function workload.

After the rollout, our team started receiving 50+ operational pages a week, including dozens overnight, because the service was load-shedding API requests. This was particularly puzzling because the instances were heavily over-provisioned, so the problem did not initially look like a straightforward capacity issue.
task: I took ownership of finding the root cause, stopping the recurring pages, and changing the architecture so background processing could no longer starve the API path.
action: The issue had already been investigated by several senior engineers, but it was difficult to pin down. The failures were intermittent, appeared mainly in larger regions, and the background jobs moved between hosts, making individual runs difficult to correlate with the API failures.

I started correlating the API load-shedding with individual background-job runs in the larger regions. One thing stood out: the jobs appeared to process surprisingly few items, yet the hosts were consuming significant CPU while they ran.

I dug into what the jobs were actually doing and found that most of the records they scanned were being filtered out locally because they did not require any work. The job was effectively scanning a large portion of the database every day, even though only a small fraction of the records were actionable.

The problem had become much worse after ZIP support was introduced. Image functions, which had originally represented almost the entire workload, had dropped to around 10% of the total volume. The background-job architecture had been designed around the old workload and was no longer scaling with the new one.

I redesigned the queries around entity state and timestamps so each host fetched only records that actually needed processing. I also deliberately bounded each execution to under a minute, preventing long-running background work from competing with the API.
Finally, I introduced state sharding and rate limiting so multiple workers could process the workload concurrently without exceeding database partition throughput limits.
result: The API load shedding and operational pages disappeared entirely. Background-job throughput increased roughly tenfold, with dynamic scaling allowing the system to handle the new workload without starving the API.

challenge: The hardest part was recognising that an apparently healthy, over-provisioned service could still be resource-starved. The system had enough overall capacity, but background work was consuming resources in a way that competed directly with latency-sensitive API traffic.
hardestBug: The signal was extremely noisy: jobs moved between hosts, the problem only appeared in a subset of regions, and even affected regions could go a day without reproducing it. There was no single failing component to follow, so I had to piece together the relationship between background-job execution and API load shedding from incomplete operational data.
differently: I would establish a clearer operational picture of the service earlier. Because it had recently been handed over from the US, I initially had to learn the meaning and limitations of existing metrics while simultaneously responding to pages. Building targeted dashboards around background-job execution and resource consumption earlier would have shortened the investigation.
aboutYourself: During one particularly intense on-call period, I realised that pride was making me try to solve too much on my own. I was running on too little sleep while trying to fight every fire myself. Since then, I've become much more conscious of recognising when I'm stretched too thin and bringing others in earlier.
enjoyed: The most satisfying part was watching the operational metrics change after the fix: page volume dropping to zero, API load shedding disappearing, and background-job throughput increasing tenfold.
